title: Popper and Kuhn: What Makes Science Science?
subtitle: Bold guesses and brutal tests, or paradigms and revolutions? Two pictures of how knowledge grows
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain the problem of demarcation and Popper's falsifiability criterion
Explain how Popper used the asymmetry between verification and falsification to sidestep Hume's problem of induction
Describe Kuhn's cycle of normal science, anomaly, crisis and revolution, and define 'paradigm' and 'incommensurability'
Compare Popper's and Kuhn's pictures of science, using historical examples such as Neptune and the oxygen revolution
Apply both views to modern debates about pseudoscience, conspiracy theories and the replication crisis
hook:
Vienna, 1919. A teenager named Karl Popper is surrounded by big theories that seem to explain everything. His friends are excited by Marx's theory of history (Day 63), by Freud's psychoanalysis, and by Alfred Adler's "individual psychology." Popper is working as a volunteer in Adler's child guidance clinics. And the more he sees, the more something bothers him. Whatever happens, the theories are confirmed. Every newspaper story confirms Marxism. Every patient confirms psychoanalysis.

That same year, a very different event makes headlines around the world. Einstein's general theory of relativity predicts that the Sun's gravity will bend starlight by a specific amount, roughly twice what Newton's physics would suggest. During a total solar eclipse on 29 May 1919, British expeditions led by Arthur Eddington photograph the stars near the darkened Sun. If the stars appear in the wrong places, Einstein's theory is finished. They appear where Einstein said they would.

The young Popper was struck by the contrast. Einstein had stuck his neck out; the other theories never did. Out of that contrast came one of the most famous ideas in modern philosophy, and a debate about the nature of science that still matters every time someone says "Trust the science."

sections.heading: Popper's Puzzle: Theories That Explain Too Much
sections.body:
Karl Popper (1902–1994) grew up in Vienna in the same intellectual world as the Vienna Circle (Day 71). He knew many of its members, but never joined; Otto Neurath called him the Circle's "official opposition."

In his famous lecture "Science: Conjectures and Refutations" (1953), Popper described what troubled him in 1919. Take two cases: a man who pushes a child into the water intending to drown it, and a man who sacrifices his life trying to save a drowning child. Freud could explain both (one man suffers from repression, the other has achieved sublimation). Adler could explain both just as easily (both men are driven by feelings of inferiority, one proving he dares to commit a crime, the other that he dares to rescue). Popper could not think of any human behavior that either theory could not explain.

He told a story about Adler himself. Popper reported a case to him that did not seem particularly Adlerian, but Adler analyzed it without difficulty in terms of his theory of inferiority feelings, without even having seen the child. When Popper asked how he could be so sure, Adler answered that it was because of his thousandfold experience. Popper recalled thinking that with this new case his experience had presumably become thousand-and-one-fold.

That was the problem. A theory that every possible observation confirms is not strong; it is empty. It tells you nothing about what will happen, because it rules nothing out. Einstein's theory, by contrast, forbade certain outcomes. It could have been caught out. That, Popper concluded, is what makes it scientific.

sections.heading: Falsifiability and the Problem of Demarcation
sections.body:
Popper called the question "What distinguishes science from non-science?" the **problem of demarcation**. His answer, set out in *Logik der Forschung* (1934), translated as *The Logic of Scientific Discovery* (1959), was **falsifiability**: a theory is scientific if and only if it makes claims that could, in principle, be shown false by observation. A scientific theory sticks its neck out. It says: if you look here, you will see this, and if you see that instead, I am wrong.

Notice how this differs from the verification principle of the logical positivists. First, Popper offered falsifiability as a test of what is *scientific*, not of what is *meaningful*. Metaphysics, for Popper, is not nonsense; many scientific ideas, like atomism (Day 7), began as metaphysical speculation. It just is not science. Second, he flipped the logic.

Remember Hume's problem of induction (Day 49). No number of observations of white swans can prove that *all* swans are white; the next one might be black. (Europeans in fact believed all swans were white until Dutch explorers encountered black swans in Australia in 1697.) So scientific laws, which are universal, can never be verified. But a single black swan conclusively refutes "All swans are white." There is an **asymmetry** between verification and falsification: universal claims can never be proven true by experience, but they can be proven false.

Popper used this asymmetry to sidestep Hume. Science, he argued, does not actually proceed by induction at all. It does not pile up observations and generalize from them. It proceeds by **conjectures and refutations**: scientists make bold guesses and then try as hard as they can to refute them. A theory that survives severe tests is **corroborated**, but never proven. It is simply the best we have so far, and it remains provisional, as Peirce's fallibilism had already suggested (Day 67).

This led to a striking claim: the best theories are the boldest ones, those that forbid the most and so run the greatest risk of being wrong. A theory that says "It will rain or not rain tomorrow" can never fail, but it is worthless. And it led Popper to criticize the theories that had troubled him in 1919. Marxism, he argued, had originally made testable predictions, such as that revolution would come first in the most industrialized countries. When those predictions failed, its followers reinterpreted both the theory and the evidence to make them fit, and so turned a once-scientific theory into an unfalsifiable dogma. Psychoanalysis, he thought, was never testable to begin with.

sections.heading: Conjectures, Refutations and the Open Society
sections.body:
Popper believed that the critical attitude of science was also the key to a decent society. In 1937, with Nazism threatening Austria, he took a teaching post in New Zealand, at Canterbury University College in Christchurch. There, far from the war, he wrote *The Open Society and Its Enemies* (1945), which he called his war effort.

Its targets were thinkers who claimed to know the laws of history and the blueprint for a perfect society: Plato's ideal city ruled by philosopher-kings (Day 14), Hegel's march of Spirit (Day 59) and Marx's historical inevitability (Day 63). Popper called this belief in inexorable laws of historical development **historicism** and argued that it led to totalitarianism: if you know where history must go, you may feel entitled to crush anyone who stands in the way. An **open society**, by contrast, treats its policies as conjectures to be tested and corrected. Its great virtue is not that it gets things right but that it allows mistakes to be discovered and leaders to be removed without bloodshed. Popper advised **piecemeal social engineering**: careful, reversible reforms whose results can be observed, rather than utopian schemes that remake everything at once.

After the war Popper moved to the London School of Economics, where he taught from 1946 until his retirement. He was knighted in 1965 and became one of the most admired philosophers among working scientists. He was also, by most accounts, a difficult man who did not take criticism of his own views well, an irony his students enjoyed pointing out. His legendary confrontation with Wittgenstein at a Cambridge seminar in 1946, in which Wittgenstein is said to have brandished a fireplace poker, is still told in conflicting versions by the people who were in the room.

sections.heading: Kuhn: Science Has a History
sections.body:
Thomas Kuhn (1922–1996) came to the philosophy of science from a different direction. He was an American physicist who earned his doctorate at Harvard and was then asked to teach the history of science to non-scientists. In 1947, preparing a class, he tried to read Aristotle's physics and found it absurd: how could such a brilliant man have been so wrong about motion? Then, by his own account, it suddenly made sense. Aristotle was not doing bad Newtonian physics. He was working with a completely different set of concepts, in which "motion" meant any kind of change, including an acorn growing into an oak. Read on its own terms, Aristotle's physics hung together.

That insight grew into *The Structure of Scientific Revolutions* (1962), one of the most widely cited academic books of the twentieth century. Ironically, it first appeared in the *International Encyclopedia of Unified Science*, the series founded by the logical positivists.

Kuhn's central concept is the **paradigm**. In its core sense, a paradigm is a shared scientific achievement, such as Newton's *Principia* or Lavoisier's chemistry, that provides a model of how to do research in a field: which problems are worth solving, which methods are acceptable, what counts as a good solution. More broadly, the word came to mean the whole framework of theories, techniques and assumptions shared by a scientific community.

Most science, Kuhn argued, is **normal science**: research conducted within an accepted paradigm. Normal scientists are not trying to overturn their theories. They are solving **puzzles**: measuring constants more precisely, extending the theory to new cases, fitting stubborn facts into the framework. When an experiment fails, the normal scientist does not conclude that the paradigm is false; she concludes that she made a mistake. And Kuhn insisted that this is not a failing. Without a firmly held paradigm, scientists would spend all their time arguing about foundations and never do the detailed, patient work that makes science advance.

sections.heading: Anomaly, Crisis and Revolution
sections.body:
Normal science does not last forever. Sometimes puzzles refuse to be solved. Kuhn called these persistent problems **anomalies**. At first they are set aside. But if they multiply, or strike at the heart of the paradigm, the field enters a period of **crisis**: confidence wavers, rival theories proliferate, scientists begin arguing about fundamentals and even turning to philosophy. Eventually a new paradigm appears that resolves the key anomalies, and the community shifts to it. That is a **scientific revolution**, or as Kuhn's phrase put it, a **paradigm shift**. Then a new period of normal science begins.

Kuhn's favorite examples included the Copernican revolution in astronomy and the chemical revolution of the 1770s and 1780s. In 1774 the English chemist Joseph Priestley isolated a gas in which candles burned brilliantly. Working within the reigning theory that burning releases a substance called phlogiston, he called it "dephlogisticated air." Antoine Lavoisier, examining the same gas, came to see it as a new element, oxygen, which combines with substances when they burn. Priestley never accepted Lavoisier's interpretation to the end of his life.

This is where Kuhn becomes radical. He argued that rival paradigms are **incommensurable**: they lack a common measure. Their key terms have different meanings ("mass" means something different for Newton and Einstein), they disagree about which problems matter, and scientists working in them in a sense see the world differently. Kuhn compared the change to a **gestalt switch**, like the famous duck-rabbit drawing: what were ducks in the scientist's world before the revolution are rabbits afterward.

If paradigms are incommensurable, the choice between them cannot be settled by a simple, neutral test. Persuasion, Kuhn suggested, plays a role, along with the passing of generations. He quoted the physicist Max Planck, who had remarked that a new scientific truth does not triumph by convincing its opponents but because the opponents eventually die and a new generation grows up familiar with it.

And science, on Kuhn's view, does not obviously progress toward the truth about nature. It certainly gets better at solving puzzles; later paradigms solve more problems than earlier ones. But Kuhn doubted that we can say successive theories come closer to the way things really are.

sections.heading: The Great Debate, and the View from Today
sections.body:
In 1965 Popper and Kuhn confronted each other at a famous conference in London, and the papers were collected in *Criticism and the Growth of Knowledge* (1970). The disagreement was sharp. For Popper, the essence of science is permanent criticism; a scientist who dutifully accepts a paradigm is, he said in effect, a person to be pitied and a danger to science. For Kuhn, Popper had described what happens only during rare revolutions and ignored the daily reality of normal science. Kuhn's critics, in turn, accused him of making science irrational, a matter of conversion and group pressure. Popper's student Imre Lakatos complained that on Kuhn's account theory change became a matter for mob psychology.

History offers evidence for both sides. In the 1840s the planet Uranus was not moving as Newton's theory predicted. On a naive Popperian view, Newton was falsified. Instead, Urbain Le Verrier in France (and, independently, John Couch Adams in England) proposed that an unseen planet was tugging on it, calculated where it should be, and in 1846 astronomers found Neptune almost exactly there. A triumph for sticking with the paradigm. But when Le Verrier tried the same trick with an anomaly in the orbit of Mercury, proposing an inner planet called Vulcan, no such planet existed. The anomaly was finally explained by Einstein's general relativity in 1915. The lesson, which the French physicist Pierre Duhem had already drawn, is that a failed prediction never refutes a theory in isolation; it shows that *something* in the whole package of theory and **auxiliary hypotheses** is wrong, without telling you which. Quine (Day 74) generalized the point.

Lakatos tried to combine Popper and Kuhn. Science consists of **research programmes** with a protected hard core and a belt of adjustable auxiliary hypotheses. A programme is **progressive** if its adjustments predict novel facts (like Neptune) and **degenerating** if they merely patch failures after the fact (like Vulcan). Lakatos's friend Paul Feyerabend went further in *Against Method* (1975), arguing that science has no single method at all; the only principle that does not inhibit progress, he provocatively said, is "anything goes."

Kuhn himself denied being a relativist. In later work he listed values that guide theory choice, including accuracy, consistency, scope, simplicity and fruitfulness. These values do not work like an algorithm, he argued, but they make theory choice reasonable rather than arbitrary. Most philosophers of science today accept something from both thinkers: Popper's insistence that good theories must risk failure, and Kuhn's insight that science is a historical, communal practice with its own structures of authority, training and resistance to change.

keyQuote.text: The criterion of the scientific status of a theory is its falsifiability, or refutability, or testability.
keyQuote.source: Karl Popper, 'Science: Conjectures and Refutations' (lecture, 1953), in Conjectures and Refutations (1963)

modernConnection.title: "Trust the Science"? Falsifiability, Paradigms and the Replication Crisis
modernConnection.body:
Popper and Kuhn give us two tools for thinking about science in the news.

Popper's tool is a pseudoscience detector. When someone defends a conspiracy theory, notice what happens to contrary evidence: the lack of evidence becomes proof of a cover-up; every debunker becomes part of the plot. Like Adler's thousandfold experience, the theory can absorb anything, and that is precisely what makes it unscientific. Ask any strong claim Popper's question: what observation would show you were wrong? If the answer is "nothing," you are not dealing with science.

Popper's ideas also shape current reforms. In 2015 a large team of researchers, the Open Science Collaboration, tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and found that only around a third or so produced clearly significant results again. Part of the problem was that researchers could analyze data in many ways after the fact until something looked impressive, a modern version of fitting theory to evidence. One remedy is **preregistration**: scientists publicly state their predictions and analysis plan before collecting data, so that a study can genuinely fail. That is falsificationism turned into lab policy.

Kuhn's tool explains why scientific change can look messy and slow. When the meteorologist Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912, most geologists rejected it, partly because he had no convincing mechanism. Only in the 1950s and 1960s, with evidence of seafloor spreading, did the field shift to plate tectonics, a textbook paradigm shift. Scientists who resist new ideas are not always fools or cowards; sometimes they are rightly demanding better evidence, and sometimes they are protecting a paradigm.

Both views warn against a naive reading of "Trust the science." Popper reminds us that scientific conclusions are always provisional, which is a strength, not a weakness: changing advice when evidence changes is science working. Kuhn reminds us that science is done by communities with their own blind spots. And the buzzword "paradigm shift," now applied to every new phone, is a good reminder that real revolutions are rare.

vocabulary.definition: The problem of finding a principled way to distinguish science from non-science and pseudoscience.
vocabulary.example: Deciding whether astrology should be taught in a science class requires an answer to the problem of demarcation.

vocabulary.definition: Popper's criterion of science: a theory is scientific only if it makes claims that some possible observation could show to be false.
vocabulary.example: 'All copper conducts electricity' meets the test of falsifiability, since one non-conducting piece of copper would refute it.

vocabulary.definition: Popper's model of scientific method: propose bold hypotheses, then subject them to severe attempts at refutation; surviving theories are corroborated but never proven.
vocabulary.example: Einstein's eclipse prediction was a bold conjecture that survived an attempted refutation.

vocabulary.definition: In Kuhn, a shared scientific achievement and the framework of theories, methods and standards it establishes for a research community.
vocabulary.example: Newtonian mechanics served as the paradigm for physics for over two centuries.

vocabulary.definition: Kuhn's term for research conducted within an accepted paradigm, aimed at solving puzzles rather than testing the paradigm itself.
vocabulary.example: Measuring a physical constant to one more decimal place is a typical task of normal science.

vocabulary.definition: A persistent observation or problem that resists explanation within the current paradigm and may, if anomalies accumulate, trigger a crisis.
vocabulary.example: The odd orbit of Mercury was an anomaly for Newtonian physics until Einstein's theory explained it.

vocabulary.definition: Kuhn's claim that rival paradigms lack a common measure, because their concepts, problems and standards differ, so choice between them cannot be settled by a simple neutral test.
vocabulary.example: Kuhn argued that 'mass' means something different in Newton's and Einstein's physics, an example of incommensurability.

vocabulary.definition: An additional assumption used alongside a main theory to derive predictions; when a prediction fails, it may be the auxiliary hypothesis rather than the theory that is at fault.
vocabulary.example: Le Verrier saved Newton's theory by adding the auxiliary hypothesis of an unseen planet, which turned out to be Neptune.

thinkingExercise.title: Is It Science? Testing Claims Like Popper and Kuhn
thinkingExercise.prompt: Apply both philosophers to claims you meet in daily life. Spend 10 to 15 minutes writing.
steps: Choose three claims: one from a science you trust (for example, about vaccines or climate), one from a field whose status is disputed (for example, astrology, a diet theory or a personality test), and one conspiracy theory or bold popular claim.
For each, write down what observation would show it to be false. Which claims make risky predictions, and which can absorb any evidence?

Take the disputed claim and imagine its defenders facing a failed prediction. Write two responses they might give: one that adds a testable auxiliary hypothesis (like Neptune) and one that merely explains the failure away (like Adler's thousandfold experience).

Now think like Kuhn: describe the 'paradigm' of a field or community you know well (your workplace, a hobby, a school subject). What does it treat as normal puzzles, and what anomalies does it tend to ignore?
Write a short verdict: whose picture of science, Popper's or Kuhn's, better fits the example you know best, and why?

summary: Popper, troubled by theories like Freud's and Adler's that could explain anything, proposed falsifiability as the criterion that demarcates science from non-science.

Exploiting the asymmetry between verification and falsification, Popper argued that science proceeds by bold conjectures and attempted refutations rather than induction, and extended this critical attitude to politics in The Open Society and Its Enemies.
Kuhn's Structure of Scientific Revolutions described science as long periods of puzzle-solving normal science within a paradigm, punctuated by crises and revolutions when anomalies accumulate.
Kuhn argued that rival paradigms are incommensurable and that theory change involves more than neutral tests, provoking charges of relativism that he denied.

Cases like Neptune and Vulcan show that failed predictions can implicate auxiliary hypotheses; Lakatos and Feyerabend developed and radicalized the debate, and today most philosophers draw on both Popper and Kuhn.

quiz.question: What made Einstein's theory scientific in Popper's eyes, compared with the theories of Freud and Adler?
options: It was more popular among intellectuals
It made a risky prediction that could have turned out false
It was based on more observations
It had been verified with certainty
quiz.explanation: The eclipse test could have refuted relativity. Popper denied that any theory is verified with certainty or that popularity matters.

quiz.question: How does Popper's falsifiability criterion differ from the logical positivists' verification principle?
options: It is a criterion of meaning rather than of science
It requires that theories be conclusively proven
It demarcates science from non-science without declaring non-science meaningless
It holds that metaphysics is the highest form of science
quiz.explanation: Popper did not think metaphysics was nonsense, only that it was not science; and he rejected the idea that scientific theories can be proven.

quiz.question: According to Popper, observing thousands of white swans proves that all swans are white.
quiz.explanation: No number of confirming instances can prove a universal law, but a single black swan can refute it: the asymmetry Popper relied on.

quiz.question: A wellness influencer claims a supplement cures fatigue. When followers report no improvement, she says their bodies were 'resisting healing'; when they feel better, the supplement worked. What would Popper say?
options: The claim is well corroborated
The claim is a successful paradigm
The claim has passed a severe test
The claim is protected from refutation and so is not scientific as defended
quiz.explanation: Like Adler's thousandfold experience, the claim absorbs every outcome, so it rules nothing out.

quiz.question: What is Kuhn's 'normal science'?
options: Research within an accepted paradigm aimed at solving puzzles
Constant attempts to overthrow the reigning theory
Science done by non-specialists
The final stage of science after all revolutions end
quiz.explanation: Normal scientists extend and refine the paradigm; failure is usually blamed on the researcher, not the paradigm.

quiz.question: Kuhn's Structure of Scientific Revolutions was first published in a series founded by the logical positivists.
quiz.explanation: It appeared in the International Encyclopedia of Unified Science, an ironic home for a book that undermined the positivist picture of science.

quiz.question: Priestley and Lavoisier studied the same gas, but Priestley called it 'dephlogisticated air' and Lavoisier called it oxygen. Which Kuhnian idea does this best illustrate?
options: Piecemeal social engineering
The asymmetry of falsification
The verification principle
Scientists working in different paradigms see and describe the same phenomena differently
quiz.explanation: Each interpreted the gas through his paradigm, like the two readings of the duck-rabbit gestalt figure.

quiz.question: What does the discovery of Neptune in 1846 show about falsification?
options: That Newton's theory was refuted
That a failed prediction can be due to a mistaken auxiliary assumption rather than the main theory
That observations cannot be trusted
That astronomy is not a science
quiz.explanation: Uranus's odd orbit was explained by adding an unseen planet, saving Newton's theory; the same move failed with Vulcan.

quiz.question: Popper's The Open Society and Its Enemies praised Plato, Hegel and Marx for discovering the laws of historical development.
quiz.explanation: Popper attacked all three as 'historicists' whose claims to know history's laws, he argued, encouraged totalitarianism.

quiz.question: According to Lakatos, what distinguishes a progressive research programme from a degenerating one?
options: Progressive programmes predict novel facts; degenerating ones only patch failures after the fact
Progressive programmes are newer
Degenerating programmes use mathematics
Progressive programmes have no auxiliary hypotheses
quiz.explanation: Neptune was a novel prediction that marked progress; Vulcan was a patch that failed.

goDeeper.body:
The Duhem–Quine thesis poses the deepest challenge to simple falsificationism. Any test of a theory relies on a web of other assumptions: about the instruments, background theories, initial conditions. When a prediction fails, logic alone tells us only that at least one assumption in the whole set is false. In principle, any single hypothesis can be saved by adjusting others. Popper knew this and responded with a methodological rule: scientists should not make ad hoc adjustments that reduce a theory's testability. Critics reply that this rule cannot be applied mechanically. Was postulating Neptune ad hoc? Only hindsight tells us it was a brilliant move rather than a desperate one.

A second debate concerns realism. Popper was a scientific realist: he believed science aims at truth and that better theories have greater 'verisimilitude,' or closeness to the truth. In 1974 David Miller and Pavel Tichý independently proved that Popper's formal definition of verisimilitude did not work: on it, no false theory could be closer to the truth than another false theory. Philosophers have been trying to repair the concept ever since. Kuhn, meanwhile, was skeptical that science converges on truth at all. The 'pessimistic meta-induction,' developed by Larry Laudan, sharpens his worry: most successful scientific theories of the past (the ether, phlogiston, caloric) turned out to be false, so why think ours are true? Realists answer with the 'no miracles' argument: if our best theories were not at least approximately true, their predictive success would be a miracle.

Finally, sociologists of scientific knowledge in the 'strong programme,' such as David Bloor, took Kuhn further than he wished, arguing that social factors explain true and false scientific beliefs alike. Kuhn himself distanced himself from them.

questions: Is there any principled way to tell when rescuing a theory with an auxiliary hypothesis is legitimate and when it is cheating?
If Kuhn is right that paradigms are incommensurable, can we still say science makes progress toward truth?
Should the public 'trust the science' if scientific conclusions are always provisional? What would wise trust look like?
